You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are a coding agent powered by the gpt-5.6-luna model.

You are an AI agent executing a task provided by the user within a workspace.

## Workspace layout

Everything you work with lives under one workspace root. **`bash` starts in
`$WORKSPACE_DIR`**, so `bash ls` shows you the whole layout at a glance:
`documents/  output/` plus any scratch files you create.

- **`$WORKSPACE_DIR`** — your working area, default `bash` cwd. Use it for
  notes and intermediate files.
- **`$DOCUMENTS_DIR`** (`$WORKSPACE_DIR/documents`) — task documents.
  Read-only.
- **`$OUTPUT_DIR`** (`$WORKSPACE_DIR/output`) — deliverables. Save every
  deliverable file here, including files you build with `bash` (.docx,
  .xlsx, .pptx): only files in `$OUTPUT_DIR` are delivered. `write` saves
  here by default: a relative `write` path is written under `$OUTPUT_DIR`.
- **Task configuration** (`task.json`) — contains the task definition and the
  grading rubric. Do not read, search, or reference it. Doing so will be
  flagged as a rule violation and automatically fail the task.

## Tool conventions

- `read` opens plain-text files only (.txt, .md, .eml, .csv, ...). To read
  .docx, .xlsx or .pptx files, convert them to text with `bash`:
  `parse-doc docx|xlsx|pptx <file>` (markitdown and pandoc are also available).
- Use `write` only for plain markdown — typically a `response.md`
  summarizing your work.
- Use `edit` for incremental refinement of a file you have already created.


Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one keeps the modification-time-ordered head.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

Use goal tools for one long-running completion objective in the current session. create_goal may infer goal intent from a direct human request in any language; do not create a goal for routine single-turn work. Call get_goal before update_goal and copy its exact goal_id and revision. After session resume or fork, an active goal is disarmed: when a human asks to continue or resume in any wording or language, use update_goal action resume to rearm it. Mark complete only when the objective is actually achieved. Mark blocked only after the same blocking condition persists for at least 3 consecutive goal rounds, and report that concrete condition in blocked_reason; difficulty, uncertainty, or useful remaining work is not blocked.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: create_goal
tools.description: Create one persisted same-session completion goal when the current direct human request is a long-running objective that should continue across autonomous goal rounds. You may infer that intent without requiring the user to say "create a goal". Do not use this for trivial single-turn work. Execution rejects non-human and subagent authority.

objective.description: The concrete completion objective inferred from the direct human request.

max_goal_rounds.description: Optional positive safe-integer limit on automatic continuation rounds.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: exit_plan_mode
tools.description: Use only in plan mode. Present your plan for the user's review and, on approval, leave plan mode. Send the COMPLETE plan as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it. The user may approve (carry out the plan from your next step) or keep planning — their feedback comes back in the tool result; revise and present again.

plan.description: The complete plan, as markdown, starting with a # heading that names it.

tools.name: get_goal
tools.description: Read the current same-session goal, including its exact id/revision, objective, phase, completed continuation rounds, round limit, blocker reason when present, and whether another continuation is armed. Call this before updating a goal.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result returns the first 100 paths in modification-time order, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: read_image
tools.description: Read a PNG/JPEG/WebP/GIF file and return the image itself. A path without a file extension is accepted; the format is detected from the file content, so normalized attachment paths can be passed directly without copying or renaming. Harness validates and downscales large supported images before the next model request, so use this tool directly instead of installing image libraries or creating thumbnails merely to inspect an image. Independent files may be read concurrently in small batches. Requires the current model to accept image input.

file_path.description: Path to the image file, resolved by the filesystem backend.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: todo_write
tools.description: Record and update a structured task list for the current work. Send the ENTIRE list every call — it REPLACES the previous list (there are no partial updates, no per-item edits). Use it to plan multi-step work and show progress: add one todo per concrete step before you start. Mark every todo being actively worked on `in_progress` — several at once when work genuinely runs in parallel (e.g. concurrent subagents or background commands), one for sequential work; while work remains, at least one task should be `in_progress`. Mark a todo `completed` the moment it is done (do not batch completions), and allow no `in_progress` item only once all work is complete. Skip the list for trivial single-step tasks. Statuses: `pending` (not started), `in_progress` (being worked on now), `completed` (finished).

todos.description: The COMPLETE task list, replacing any previous list.

content.description: What the task is — a short imperative line.

tools.name: update_goal
tools.description: Update the exact current goal revision. edit, pause, and resume require a direct top-level human request. During an automatic continuation of the current goal, complete and blocked are also allowed. blocked is rejected before the configured minimum round count; the model remains responsible for judging that the same condition persisted across those rounds and must explain it in blocked_reason.

revision.description: Exact positive revision returned by get_goal.

objective.description: Replacement objective; valid only with action edit.

max_goal_rounds.description: Replacement cap; valid only with action edit.

blocked_reason.description: Concrete blocking condition; required only with action blocked.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file. A relative path is written under the output directory (`output/`): `response.md` is saved as `output/response.md`. An absolute path is used as is.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

**Must-have:** Liability must be **uncapped** for the following categories of claims:

> \(a\) **Willful misconduct** by vendor, its employees, agents, or subprocessors;
>
> \(b\) **Gross negligence** by vendor, its employees, agents, or subprocessors;
>
> \(c\) **Breaches of confidentiality obligations** involving intentional or reckless conduct; and
>
> \(d\) **Regulatory fines or penalties** imposed on Pinnacle as a direct result of vendor\'s non-compliance with applicable data protection laws, including HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR.

**Must-have:** Consequential, indirect, and special damages may **NOT** be excluded for data breaches involving willful misconduct by vendor. A blanket consequential damages exclusion that applies to all claims, including data protection claims, is unacceptable. While mutual exclusions of consequential damages are common in general commercial agreements, they are inappropriate in the data protection context where the most significant harms to Pinnacle --- including regulatory penalties, class action settlements, breach notification costs, credit monitoring expenses, and reputational damage --- may be characterized as consequential or indirect damages under applicable law. A blanket exclusion could effectively eliminate vendor accountability for the very harms the DPA is intended to address.

**Nice-to-have:** A separate, higher \"**super-cap**\" for data protection claims (e.g., **3x annual fees**) that sits above the general MSA liability cap. This approach allows the parties to maintain a standard liability cap for general commercial claims under the MSA while providing enhanced protection for data protection claims under the DPA. For example, where annual fees are \$4.2 million, the general MSA cap might be \$4.2 million (1x) while the DPA super-cap would be \$12.6 million (3x).

**Fallback:** If vendor insists on a single aggregate cap covering both general commercial claims and data protection claims, the minimum acceptable cap is **2x total annual fees** (\$8,400,000 for a \$4.2 million annual engagement). Pinnacle will not accept a DPA liability cap below this threshold. Any vendor proposal below 2x annual fees must be escalated to Margaret Yuen-Park for review and decision.

**Note for negotiators:** Vendor templates frequently propose caps that are a small fraction of annual fees. It is not uncommon for a vendor with annual fees of several million dollars to propose a DPA liability cap of €500,000 or \$1,000,000. Such caps are commercially unreasonable given the regulatory exposure described above and the volume of data at stake. Negotiators should be prepared to provide the regulatory exposure calculations above as support for Pinnacle\'s 2x annual fees position.

**[6.2 Indemnification]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** Vendor must indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Pinnacle, its officers, directors, employees, agents, and affiliates (including Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.) from and against all losses, damages, liabilities, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys\' fees and costs of litigation) arising from or related to:

> \(a\) **Third-party claims** (including claims by data subjects, consumers, patients, and healthcare providers) arising from vendor\'s breach of the DPA, the BAA, or any applicable data protection law;
>
> \(b\) **Regulatory fines, penalties, assessments, and enforcement costs** imposed on Pinnacle by any governmental authority (including HHS OCR, the California Attorney General, the California Privacy Protection Agency, and any EU/EEA supervisory authority) arising from or related to vendor\'s non-compliance with applicable data protection laws; and
>
> \(c\) **Costs of breach response**, including but not limited to: costs of breach notification to affected individuals and regulatory authorities; costs of credit monitoring and identity theft protection services provided to affected individuals; costs of forensic investigation; costs of public relations and crisis communications; and costs of regulatory reporting and compliance remediation, in each case to the extent arising from vendor\'s breach of the DPA, the BAA, or applicable data protection law.

Indemnification obligations should be subject to the same uncapped/capped structure as direct liability set forth in Section 6.1 above. Specifically, indemnification for claims arising from willful misconduct, gross negligence, intentional breaches of confidentiality, and regulatory fines resulting from vendor non-compliance must be uncapped. Indemnification for all other claims may be subject to the aggregate liability cap (2x annual fees), but must not be subject to any lower cap or sublimit.

Vendor\'s indemnification obligations must be in addition to, and not in limitation of, any other rights or remedies available to Pinnacle at law or in equity.

**[Section 7: CCPA / CPRA Service Provider Requirements]{.underline}**

This Section sets forth the mandatory contractual provisions that must appear in all DPAs where the vendor processes personal information of California residents on Pinnacle\'s behalf. These provisions are required to establish the vendor\'s status as a \"Service Provider\" under the CCPA/CPRA, which is essential to Pinnacle\'s compliance with the statute.

**[7.1 Service Provider Contractual Terms]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** The DPA must include the following CCPA/CPRA Service Provider provisions, consistent with Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d) and § 1798.140(ag):

> **(a) Prohibition on Selling or Sharing.** Vendor is prohibited from selling (as defined in Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ad)) or sharing (as defined in Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ah)) any personal information received from, or on behalf of, Pinnacle. This prohibition applies regardless of whether the vendor receives monetary or other valuable consideration in exchange for the personal information.
>
> **(b) Purpose Limitation.** Vendor is prohibited from retaining, using, or disclosing personal information received from Pinnacle for any purpose other than performing the services specified in the DPA and the applicable MSA, including any commercial purpose other than providing the services specified in the agreement. Vendor may not use Pinnacle\'s personal information for vendor\'s own business purposes, including but not limited to marketing, product development, analytics, or profiling, unless such use is expressly authorized by Pinnacle in writing and is consistent with a permissible business purpose under the CCPA/CPRA.
>
> **(c) Restriction to Direct Business Relationship.** Vendor is prohibited from retaining, using, or disclosing personal information received from Pinnacle outside of the direct business relationship between Pinnacle and vendor. This means that vendor may not use Pinnacle\'s personal information to provide services to any other client or customer of vendor, or for any purpose unrelated to the services vendor provides to Pinnacle under the DPA/MSA.
>
> **(d) Prohibition on Combining.** Vendor is prohibited from combining personal information received from Pinnacle with personal information that vendor receives from or on behalf of any other person or entity, or that vendor collects from the consumer\'s own direct interaction with the vendor, except as expressly permitted by the CCPA/CPRA (e.g., to detect data security incidents or protect against fraud).
>
> **(e) Service Provider Certification.** Vendor must include a certification, executed by an authorized representative of vendor, stating that vendor understands the restrictions set forth in subparagraphs (a) through (d) above and will comply with them. This certification is a statutory requirement under the CPRA amendments to Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d) and must appear in the DPA itself or in a CCPA/CPRA Addendum appended to the DPA.
>
> **(f) Right to Monitor Compliance.** Vendor must grant Pinnacle the right to take reasonable and appropriate steps to help ensure that vendor uses personal information in a manner consistent with Pinnacle\'s obligations under the CCPA/CPRA. This includes the right to conduct ongoing manual reviews, automated scans, and assessments of vendor\'s systems and practices as they relate to the processing of personal information received from Pinnacle.
>
> **(g) Notification of Inability to Comply.** Vendor must notify Pinnacle promptly if vendor determines that it can no longer meet its obligations under the CCPA/CPRA. Upon receipt of such notification, Pinnacle shall have the right to take reasonable and appropriate steps to stop and remediate the unauthorized use of personal information, up to and including termination of the DPA/MSA.

**Nice-to-have:** Vendor agrees to cooperate with Pinnacle in responding to CCPA/CPRA consumer requests, including the right to know (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.110), the right to delete (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.105), the right to correct (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.106), and the right to opt-out of sale/sharing (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.120), within timelines consistent with the statute. Under the CCPA/CPRA, Pinnacle must respond to consumer requests within **forty-five (45) days**, with a **forty-five (45) day extension** upon notice to the consumer. Vendor\'s cooperation must be sufficiently prompt to allow Pinnacle to meet these deadlines.

**Fallback:** If the vendor\'s DPA template contains no CCPA/CPRA provisions whatsoever, Pinnacle will require a **standalone CCPA/CPRA Addendum** appended to the DPA. The addendum must contain all of the provisions listed in subparagraphs (a) through (g) above and must be expressly incorporated into the DPA by reference. The negotiator should use the template language provided in Appendix B as a starting point for drafting the addendum.

**[7.2 California Consumer Volume]{.underline}**

As of February 2025, Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately **890,000 California residents** across its patient platform, provider network, and associated data processing activities. This volume is expected to grow as Pinnacle\'s US user base expands. All vendors with access to California resident personal information, regardless of the volume of records processed by any individual vendor, must comply with the requirements set forth in Section 7.1 above.

**[Section 8: Audit Rights]{.underline}**

Audit provisions are a cornerstone of any effective DPA. Pinnacle\'s ability to verify vendor compliance with HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR depends on having contractual audit rights that are robust enough to cover all data processing locations, including subprocessor facilities, and all relevant compliance domains. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s audit right requirements.

**[8.1 Scope of Audit Rights]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** Pinnacle must have the contractual right to audit vendor\'s data processing activities, directly or through a qualified third-party auditor designated by Pinnacle. The scope of the audit right must include:

> **(a) All data center locations** where Pinnacle data is stored or processed. Audit rights must not be limited to the vendor\'s primary data center; they must extend to all locations, including secondary, disaster recovery, and backup sites.
>
> **(b) All subprocessor facilities** where Pinnacle data is stored or processed. This requirement is critical where subprocessors operate in different jurisdictions from the vendor (e.g., a US subprocessor handling EU data under a Processor-to-Subprocessor transfer). Subprocessor audit coverage is essential to verifying end-to-end compliance with the data protection requirements applicable to Pinnacle\'s data.
>
> **(c) Vendor\'s policies, procedures, and technical controls** relevant to data protection, including but not limited to: information security policies, access control procedures, incident response plans, data classification policies, encryption configurations, and vulnerability management programs.
>
> **(d) Vendor\'s compliance with HIPAA Security Rule safeguards** specifically, including administrative safeguards (45 CFR § 164.308), physical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.310), and technical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.312), where vendor is a Business Associate.

**Must-have:** Audit rights must extend to subprocessor locations. Vendor must provide Pinnacle with one of the following mechanisms for subprocessor audit coverage:

> \(i\) Vendor grants Pinnacle **direct audit rights** over subprocessor facilities, with the same scope and frequency as Pinnacle\'s audit rights over vendor; or
>
> \(ii\) Vendor **contractually requires** each subprocessor to submit to audits by Pinnacle or Pinnacle\'s designated auditor, and provides Pinnacle with the contractual right to exercise such audits; or
>
> \(iii\) At minimum, vendor requires each subprocessor to **provide SOC 2 Type II reports** and/or **ISO 27001 certifications** covering the relevant data processing services, with copies provided to Pinnacle upon request no less frequently than annually.

**Nice-to-have:** Pinnacle prefers the right to conduct **two (2) audits per calendar year**: one planned audit and one for-cause audit. Planned audits should require **fifteen (15) days\' prior written notice** to the vendor. For-cause audits, triggered by a breach, suspected breach, or other compliance concern, should require **no advance notice** to the vendor.

**Fallback:** One (1) planned audit per calendar year with **thirty (30) days\' prior written notice** is acceptable, provided that the following conditions are met:

> \(a\) For-cause audits are permitted **without notice** following a confirmed or suspected breach, a regulatory inquiry, or a material compliance concern identified by Pinnacle;
>
> \(b\) Audit scope extends to **all data processing locations**, including subprocessor sites, as described above;
>
> \(c\) Vendor provides **current SOC 2 Type II reports** and **ISO 27001 certifications** as a supplement to (not a replacement for) on-site audits, with reports and certifications provided to Pinnacle within thirty (30) days of request; and
>
> \(d\) Vendor cooperates fully with the audit, including by providing access to relevant personnel, documentation, and systems, and by making reasonable workspace available to Pinnacle\'s audit team during on-site audits.

**Red line:** Audit rights limited to a single vendor facility (excluding subprocessor sites) are **unacceptable**. Such a limitation would prevent Pinnacle from verifying compliance at the locations where data processing actually occurs, particularly where the vendor relies on subprocessors for hosting, storage, or processing activities. If vendor refuses to extend audit scope to subprocessor facilities, the negotiator must escalate immediately to Margaret Yuen-Park.

**[8.2 HIPAA Audit Requirements]{.underline}**

Under HIPAA, Pinnacle as Covered Entity must be able to audit Business Associates for compliance with the HIPAA Security Rule and Privacy Rule. The DPA/BAA must expressly state that Pinnacle\'s audit rights include the right to evaluate vendor\'s HIPAA compliance, including without limitation:

> • Review of vendor\'s HIPAA risk assessments (required under 45 CFR § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A));
>
> • Review of vendor\'s workforce training records and training content;
>
> • Review of vendor\'s security incident logs and breach response records;
>
> • Review of vendor\'s policies and procedures related to PHI access, use, disclosure, and safeguarding;
>
> • Interviews with vendor\'s HIPAA Privacy Officer and HIPAA Security Officer (or equivalents); and
>
> • Inspection of physical and technical safeguards at facilities where ePHI is created, received, maintained, or transmitted.

The HIPAA audit right must be independent of and in addition to any general audit right under the DPA. If the DPA\'s general audit provision is narrower than what HIPAA requires, the BAA must include a separate, broader audit provision that addresses the HIPAA-specific requirements listed above.

**[Section 9: Data Return, Deletion, and Retention]{.underline}**

This Section addresses the provisions governing the disposition of data at the end of the vendor relationship, including the critical interplay between post-termination data deletion obligations and HIPAA\'s six-year record retention requirement. Getting these provisions right is essential to ensuring both a clean transition and ongoing regulatory compliance.

**[9.1 Data Return Option]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** Upon termination or expiration of the DPA/MSA, for any reason, vendor must provide Pinnacle with a **data return option** --- that is, the right to receive a complete copy of all Personal Data, PHI, and California Personal Information processed by vendor under the DPA, in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format, before any deletion occurs. The data return option must be exercisable at Pinnacle\'s sole election; vendor may not condition the return of data on payment of additional fees beyond those specified in the DPA/MSA, nor may vendor require Pinnacle to waive any rights or claims as a condition of data return.

**Must-have:** Vendor must provide **at least thirty (30) calendar days of transition assistance** following Pinnacle\'s request for data return, during which period vendor must: (i) continue to securely host and maintain Pinnacle\'s data in accordance with all security and confidentiality obligations of the DPA; (ii) cooperate in data migration activities, including by making data available for export through secure channels and in agreed-upon formats; (iii) make relevant vendor personnel available to support the transition, including technical staff familiar with the data structures and systems involved; and (iv) refrain from deleting any Pinnacle data until Pinnacle has confirmed in writing that the data return is complete.

**Must-have:** Following completion of data return (or upon Pinnacle\'s written instruction to proceed directly to deletion without return), vendor must **securely delete all copies** of Pinnacle data in vendor\'s possession, custody, or control, including copies in active systems, staging environments, archives, and backup media. Pinnacle\'s playbook target is deletion within **thirty (30) calendar days** following completion of data return or receipt of Pinnacle\'s deletion instruction; the maximum acceptable deletion window is **sixty (60) calendar days**. Vendor must provide Pinnacle with a **written certification of deletion** signed by an authorized officer of vendor, confirming that all copies of Pinnacle data have been securely deleted using methods consistent with NIST SP 800-88 or equivalent standards.

**Nice-to-have:** Vendor provides data return in Pinnacle\'s preferred format (to be specified in the DPA or MSA), with all metadata intact and in a structure that facilitates import into Pinnacle\'s systems or a successor vendor\'s systems without material data loss or reformatting.

**Fallback:** If vendor insists on a longer deletion window (e.g., 90 days), this is acceptable only if: (i) the data return option is fully preserved; (ii) the 30-day transition assistance period is preserved; (iii) all security, confidentiality, and use restrictions of the DPA continue to apply to retained data throughout the extended deletion window; and (iv) vendor provides a written explanation of why 90 days is required (e.g., backup media rotation schedules).

**[9.2 HIPAA Record Retention]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** The DPA/BAA must acknowledge and account for HIPAA\'s **six (6) year record retention requirement** under 45 CFR § 164.530(j). Vendor must retain HIPAA-required documentation for six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when the document was last in effect, whichever is later. The categories of documentation subject to this requirement include:

> • The BAA itself;
>
> • Policies and procedures related to the privacy and security of PHI;
>
> • Workforce training records and training materials;
>
> • Security incident and breach response records;
>
> • Risk assessments and risk management documentation;
>
> • Access logs and audit trails related to PHI; and
>
> • Any other documentation required to demonstrate compliance with HIPAA requirements.

**Must-have:** The six-year HIPAA retention obligation must be **expressly reconciled** with the post-termination deletion obligation set forth in Section 9.1 above. Without an express reconciliation, the deletion obligation and the retention obligation create an internal contradiction that could result in either premature deletion of HIPAA-required records or indefinite retention of PHI without adequate contractual protections. Pinnacle\'s recommended reconciliation language is as follows:

> *\"Notwithstanding the deletion obligations in this Section, Processor shall retain such records as are required to comply with HIPAA record retention requirements (45 CFR § 164.530(j)) for a period of six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when such records were last in effect, whichever is later. Such retained records shall remain subject to the confidentiality, security, and use restrictions of this Agreement and the Business Associate Agreement for the duration of the retention period. Upon expiration of the applicable retention period, Processor shall securely delete all such retained records and provide Controller with written certification of deletion.\"*

**Red line:** Any post-termination deletion clause that does not carve out HIPAA record retention requirements is **non-compliant** and creates significant regulatory risk. A vendor that deletes HIPAA-required documentation within 30 or 60 days of termination may be in violation of 45 CFR § 164.530(j), and Pinnacle could face enforcement consequences if it cannot produce required documentation during an OCR investigation. Negotiators must ensure that the HIPAA retention carve-out is included in every DPA involving PHI. If a vendor\'s DPA template contains a blanket deletion-at-termination clause without a HIPAA carve-out, the clause must be redlined before execution. Escalate immediately if the vendor refuses to include the carve-out.

**[Section 10: Governing Law and Dispute Resolution]{.underline}**

Governing law and dispute resolution provisions are critical in DPAs that cover both US and EU data, particularly where the vendor is a non-US entity. A DPA that applies a single non-US governing law and non-US dispute resolution forum to all disputes --- including disputes involving US PHI and California personal information --- could undermine Pinnacle\'s ability to enforce its US regulatory rights and may be inconsistent with the jurisdictional framework of HIPAA and CCPA/CPRA enforcement. This Section establishes Pinnacle\'s required approach: a bifurcated governing law and dispute resolution structure.

**[10.1 Bifurcated Governing Law]{.underline}**

**Must-have:** DPAs covering both US and EU data must include a **bifurcated governing law clause** that applies different governing law depending on the nature of the claim and the data involved:

> **(a) US Data Disputes.** All disputes, claims, and obligations arising from or related to the processing of **US data** --- including PHI, ePHI, CCPA/CPRA-covered personal information, and any other personal data of US-based data subjects --- shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the **State of Delaware**, without regard to its conflict of laws principles. Delaware law is Pinnacle\'s preferred governing law for US data disputes because Pinnacle is a Delaware corporation, Delaware has a well-developed body of commercial law, and the Delaware courts have extensive experience with complex commercial and data-related disputes.
>
> **(b) EU/EEA Data Disputes.** All disputes, claims, and obligations arising from or related to the processing of **EU/EEA data** --- including GDPR-covered personal data of EU/EEA data subjects --- shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the **applicable EU/EEA Member State**. Where Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V. is the contracting controller, the law of the **Netherlands** is preferred. Where the vendor is based in Germany and strongly resists Dutch law, **German law** is an acceptable alternative for EU data disputes.

**Nice-to-have:** Delaware law for all matters, including EU data disputes. However, this position is unlikely to be accepted by EU-based vendors and may conflict with GDPR mandatory provisions that require application of EU Member State law for certain data protection matters,  and remediation activities provided to Pinnacle. This is market standard and should be readily achievable by any vendor with a mature security program. Vendor should also agree to implement additional security measures as reasonably requested by Pinnacle to address evolving threats, emerging vulnerabilities, or changes in applicable law or regulatory guidance.

**[Section 14: Data Subject / Consumer Rights Assistance]{.underline}**

Pinnacle has obligations under HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA, and GDPR to respond to requests from individuals (patients, consumers, and data subjects) exercising their data protection rights. Because vendors often hold or process the data necessary to respond to these requests, vendor cooperation is essential. This Section sets forth the requirements for vendor assistance with data subject and consumer rights requests.

**Must-have:** Vendor must assist Pinnacle in responding to data subject and consumer rights requests under all applicable regulatory regimes, including but not limited to:

> **HIPAA --- Individual Access Rights.** Under 45 CFR § 164.524, individuals have the right to access their PHI. Pinnacle must provide access within **thirty (30) days** of the request, with one **thirty (30) day extension** permitted upon written notice to the individual. Vendor must cooperate with Pinnacle to identify, locate, and produce the requested PHI within a timeframe that enables Pinnacle to meet this regulatory deadline.
>
> **CCPA/CPRA --- Consumer Rights.** Under the CCPA/CPRA, California consumers have the right to know (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.110), the right to delete (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.105), the right to correct (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.106), the right to opt-out of sale/sharing (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.120), and the right to limit use of sensitive personal information (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.121). Pinnacle must respond to consumer requests within **forty-five (45) days**, with a **forty-five (45) day extension** upon notice to the consumer. Vendor must assist Pinnacle in fulfilling these requests, including by searching vendor\'s systems for the consumer\'s personal information, executing deletion or correction instructions, and confirming completion.
>
> **GDPR --- Data Subject Rights.** Under the GDPR, data subjects have the right of access (Art. 15), the right to rectification (Art. 16), the right to erasure (Art. 17), the right to restriction of processing (Art. 18), the right to data portability (Art. 20), and the right to object (Art. 21). Pinnacle/Pinnacle EU B.V. must respond to data subject requests within **thirty (30) days** per GDPR Art. 12(3), with a possible extension of two additional months for complex or numerous requests. Vendor must assist Pinnacle in responding within this timeframe.

**Must-have:** Vendor\'s assistance timeline must be **short enough** to allow Pinnacle to meet its own regulatory deadlines. Given the regulatory timelines above, vendor delay in responding to Pinnacle\'s requests for assistance could result in Pinnacle missing a statutory deadline, with potential enforcement consequences.

**Nice-to-have:** Vendor responds to Pinnacle\'s data subject/consumer rights assistance requests within **five (5) business days** of receipt. This provides Pinnacle with a meaningful buffer before its own regulatory deadlines expire.

**Fallback:** A response timeline of **ten (10) business days** is acceptable, provided that vendor commits to best efforts to respond sooner where Pinnacle indicates that the request is time-sensitive.

**[Section 15: DPA Term, Survival, and Termination Provisions]{.underline}**

This Section addresses the DPA\'s term, its relationship to the underlying MSA, and the critical question of which provisions survive termination and for how long.

**Must-have:** The DPA should be **coterminous with the MSA**. The DPA should become effective upon execution of the MSA (or, if later, upon the date the vendor first processes Pinnacle data) and should remain in effect until the MSA terminates or expires, unless terminated earlier in accordance with its terms. If the MSA is renewed or extended, the DPA should automatically renew or extend for the same period.

**Must-have:** The following DPA provisions must **survive termination** of the DPA and the MSA for a period sufficient to cover all applicable regulatory obligations:

> • **Breach notification** obligations (Section 5);
>
> • **Data return and deletion** obligations (Section 9);
>
> • **Liability and indemnification** obligations (Section 6);
>
> • **Audit rights** (Section 8), to the extent necessary to verify compliance with post-termination obligations;
>
> • **Confidentiality** obligations, for as long as vendor retains any Pinnacle data; and
>
> • **HIPAA BAA obligations**, for as long as vendor retains any PHI, and in any event for the six (6) year record retention period under 45 CFR § 164.530(j).

**Note on HIPAA Survival:** HIPAA requires six (6) years of record retention under 45 CFR § 164.530(j). Any DPA survival period shorter than six (6) years may be insufficient for HIPAA purposes, because the termination of the DPA\'s protective provisions before the end of the retention period would leave PHI-related documentation without contractual protections. Where a vendor proposes a shorter survival period (e.g., two (2) years), Pinnacle must negotiate either:

> \(a\) An extension of the general DPA survival period to six (6) years; or
>
> \(b\) A carve-out providing that HIPAA-related obligations (including the BAA, security obligations, audit rights, and confidentiality obligations as they relate to PHI) survive for the full **six (6) year retention period** or for as long as vendor retains any PHI, whichever is longer, even if the general DPA survival period is shorter.

**Fallback:** A general DPA survival period of **two (2) to three (3) years** is acceptable for non-HIPAA obligations, provided that HIPAA obligations have a separate, longer survival as described above. The negotiator should ensure that the survival clause clearly distinguishes between the general survival period and the HIPAA-specific survival period, and that the HIPAA survival is not inadvertently overridden by the general survival provision.

**Note for legal review regarding Orionis:** The DPA Template describes Orionis\'s services as \"anonymization and analytics.\" However, the DPA does not define or distinguish between \"anonymization\" and \"pseudonymization.\" This omission creates significant regulatory ambiguity. Under the GDPR, truly anonymized data falls outside the scope of the Regulation entirely (Recital 26), meaning that once data has been effectively and irreversibly anonymized, no GDPR obligations attach to its further processing, storage, or transfer. By contrast, pseudonymized data remains personal data subject to the full scope of GDPR obligations (Article 4(5), Recital 26).

The standard for effective anonymization established in Article 29 Working Party Opinion 05/2014 on Anonymisation Techniques (WP216, now endorsed by the European Data Protection Board) requires that data be rendered irreversibly incapable of identifying a data subject, considering all means reasonably likely to be used. The WP29 Opinion establishes a three-criteria test assessing the risks of (i) singling out, (ii) linkability, and (iii) inference. Data that does not satisfy all three criteria cannot be considered truly anonymized.

If Orionis\'s processing produces pseudonymized rather than truly anonymized outputs, those outputs remain personal data subject to the GDPR and must be covered by the DPA\'s processing terms. This includes all obligations related to international transfer mechanisms (if the data were subsequently transferred outside the EEA), security measures, data retention limitations, data subject rights facilitation, and breach notification. The DPA should define the anonymization standard by reference to objective and verifiable criteria, specify validation and certification requirements for Orionis\'s outputs, and expressly address the regulatory consequences if true anonymization is not achieved in practice.

**[Section 3: Data Flow Diagrams]{.underline}**

This section provides detailed textual descriptions of each data flow between and among the parties identified in Section 1. **[3.1 Diagram 1 --- EU Data Flow (Primary Processing)]{.underline}**

**Flow Description:**

The primary EU data flow originates at **Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.** (Amsterdam, Netherlands), acting in its capacity as Controller. EU patient data and EU healthcare provider contact data are transmitted via encrypted connection using Transport Layer Security (TLS) version 1.3 to two destinations within the European Economic Area:

**Destination 1:** The data is transmitted to the **Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH Frankfurt Data Center** located in Frankfurt, Germany. This facility serves as the primary storage location for all EU personal data. Data is encrypted at rest using AES-256 encryption. Stratosphere acts as Processor at this location.

**Destination 2:** The data is simultaneously or subsequently replicated to the **Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH Dublin Data Center** located in Dublin, Ireland. This facility serves as the redundant storage and failover location for EU personal data. Data is encrypted at rest using AES-256 encryption. Stratosphere acts as Processor at this location.

**Intra-EEA Transfer:** The data replication between the Frankfurt data center and the Dublin data center constitutes an intra-EEA transfer. Both Germany and Ireland are Member States of the European Union and part of the European Economic Area. No international transfer mechanism under GDPR Chapter V is required for this data flow.

**Processing Activities:** Cloud hosting, managed database services, structured and unstructured data storage, scheduled and on-demand backup, system monitoring, and performance optimization.

**Transfer Mechanism Required:** None --- this is an intra-EEA processing arrangement.

**[3.2 Diagram 2 --- US Data Flow (Primary Processing)]{.underline}**

**Flow Description:**

The primary US data flow originates at **Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc.** (Austin, TX), acting in its capacity as HIPAA Covered Entity and Controller. US patient PHI and US healthcare provider contact data are transmitted via encrypted connection using TLS 1.3 to a single destination within the United States:

**Destination:** The data is transmitted to the **Northern Virginia Data Center** located in Fairfax, Virginia, which is owned and operated by **Larkfield Data Systems, LLC**. Larkfield acts as a Subprocessor under the GDPR framework and as a Business Associate sub-contractor under HIPAA. Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH accesses and manages the data hosted at the Larkfield Northern Virginia facility pursuant to the terms of the MSA.

**Processing Activities:** Database management, disaster recovery services, structured and unstructured data storage, scheduled and on-demand backup, data replication for business continuity purposes, and system monitoring.

**Cross-Border Transfer:** All US data remains within the United States throughout this data flow. No cross-border or international transfer occurs in connection with primary US processing. Accordingly, no GDPR Chapter V transfer mechanism is required.

**Regulatory Note:** Although no GDPR international transfer mechanism is required for this flow, the HIPAA Business Associate Agreement (\"BAA\") obligations must flow down from Stratosphere to Larkfield. The adequacy of this BAA flow-down is addressed in the separate compliance gap memorandum and is not within the scope of this data flow document.

**[3.3 Diagram 3 --- Cross-Border Transfer: Frankfurt to Northern Virginia (Disaster Recovery)]{.underline}**

**Flow Description:**

This data flow involves the transfer of EU-originating data from within the EEA to a facility located in the United States. It constitutes an international transfer of personal data under GDPR Chapter V and requires a valid transfer mechanism.

**Source:** The data originates from the **Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH Frankfurt Data Center** (Frankfurt, Germany), where Stratosphere acts as Processor within the EEA. The datasets transferred consist of aggregated and pseudonymized datasets derived from EU personal data originally provided by Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.

**Transmission:** The data is transmitted via encrypted connection to the destination facility. The DPA Template does not specify the encryption protocol for this particular transfer; counsel should confirm that TLS 1.3 or equivalent encryption is applied.

**Destination:** The data is received at the **Northern Virginia Data Center** (Fairfax, VA), operated by **Larkfield Data Systems, LLC**. Larkfield acts as Subprocessor. The data center is located outside the European Economic Area.

**Purpose:** Disaster recovery and business continuity. The transferred datasets are maintained at the Northern Virginia facility to ensure service continuity in the event of a catastrophic failure at the Frankfurt or Dublin data centers.

**Transfer Mechanism in DPA Template:** The DPA Template (Section 7) references the EU Standard Contractual Clauses adopted pursuant to Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 of June 4, 2021. However, the DPA Template attaches only **Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor)** of the 2021 SCCs.

**FLAG FOR LEGAL REVIEW --- Transfer Mechanism Gap :** This transfer is from **Stratosphere (Processor)** to **Larkfield (Subprocessor)**. The DPA Template attaches only SCC Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor), which governs transfers from a Controller to a Processor. However, this specific transfer is a Processor-to-Subprocessor transfer, which requires **SCC Module 3 (Processor-to-Subprocessor)** under Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914. The 2021 SCCs contain four modules designed for distinct transfer scenarios: Module 1 (Controller-to-Controller), Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor), Module 3 (Processor-to-Subprocessor), and Module 4 (Processor-to-Controller). Module 2 alone is legally insufficient for this transfer scenario. Module 3 must be separately executed between Stratosphere (as data exporter/Processor) and Larkfield (as data importer/Subprocessor), with Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V. as the ultimate Controller having enforceable rights under the SCCs as a third-party beneficiary. The failure to include Module 3 means there is currently no valid transfer mechanism in place for this data flow.

**FLAG FOR LEGAL REVIEW --- Larkfield DPF Status :** Larkfield Data Systems, LLC is **NOT** certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. The European Commission\'s adequacy decision for the DPF (adopted July 10, 2023) can only be relied upon where the data importer is a certified participant in the DPF program. Because Larkfield has not obtained DPF certification, the DPF adequacy decision cannot serve as an alternative transfer mechanism for this transfer. SCCs (with the correct Module 3 selection) remain the only viable mechanism for this transfer, unless Larkfield obtains DPF certification prior to the September 1, 2025 go-live date.

**FLAG FOR LEGAL REVIEW --- No Transfer Impact Assessment :** The DPA Template does not require, reference, or document any Transfer Impact Assessment (\"TIA\") for this transfer. Following the Court of Justice of the European Union\'s judgment in *Data Protection Commissioner v. Facebook Ireland Limited and Maximillian Schrenk* (Case C-311/18, \"Schrems II,\" July 16, 2020) and the EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 on measures that supplement transfer tools to ensure compliance with the EU level of protection of personal data (Version 2.0, adopted June 18, 2021), a TIA is required to assess whether the legal framework in the destination country (here, the United States) provides an essentially equivalent level of protection for personal data. The TIA must specifically assess US surveillance laws (including Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act and Executive Order 12333), the availability of redress mechanisms (including those established by Executive Order 14086 and the Data Protection Review Court), and any supplementary technical, organizational, or contractual measures needed to address identified risks. No TIA has been prepared, referenced, or required by the DPA Template for any international transfer.

**Additional Note Regarding Pseudonymized Data:** Although the datasets transferred to the Northern Virginia facility are described in the DPA Template as \"aggregated and pseudonymized,\" it is essential to recognize that pseudonymized data remains personal data under the GDPR (Article 4(5), Recital 26) and requires a valid transfer mechanism under Chapter V. Only data that has been truly and irreversibly anonymized in accordance with the standard articulated in WP29 Opinion 05/2014 (WP216) would fall outside the scope of the GDPR and thereby not require a transfer mechanism. The characterization of data as \"pseudonymized\" does not reduce or eliminate the requirement for SCCs or another valid transfer mechanism. See also the flag regarding Orionis and the anonymization/pseudonymization distinction in Section 1.3 above.

**[3.4 Diagram 4 --- Cross-Border Access: Singapore Remote Access to EU Data]{.underline}**

**Flow Description:**

This data flow involves remote access by Stratosphere personnel located outside the EEA to EU personal data stored within the EEA. Although no data is physically transferred to or stored in Singapore, remote access from a third country constitutes a \"transfer\" of personal data under the GDPR, as confirmed by EDPB guidance.

**Accessor:** **Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH support engineers based in Singapore.** These individuals are employees or contractors of Stratosphere acting in their capacity as Processor personnel. Singapore is not an EU Member State and is not part of the European Economic Area.

**Access Method:** Remote access via encrypted VPN tunnel using TLS 1.3 to the Frankfurt and/or Dublin data centers. The Singapore-based engineers access EU personal data for the purposes of incident resolution and technical support. Data is viewed and, in some cases, modified remotely but is not copied to or stored at any Singapore facility.

**Data Location:** The EU personal data remains physically stored at the **Stratosphere Frankfurt Data Center** (Germany) and/or the **Stratosphere Dublin Data Center** (Ireland), both within the EEA.

**Purpose:** Incident resolution, technical troubleshooting, and technical support services.

**Nature of Access as International Transfer:** Although the data is not physically relocated to Singapore, remote access from a third country to personal data stored within the EEA constitutes an international transfer under the GDPR within the meaning of Chapter V. The EDPB has consistently treated such remote access scenarios as transfers requiring a valid legal mechanism. Singapore is not covered by an EU adequacy decision under Article 45 GDPR.

**FLAG FOR LEGAL REVIEW --- Singapore Access Not Addressed :** The DPA Template does not address the Singapore remote access scenario at all. DPA Section 7, which governs international transfers, is entirely silent on the existence of Stratosphere personnel in Singapore and on any remote access from Singapore to EU personal data stored in Frankfurt or Dublin. This constitutes a compliance gap.

Because Singapore is not the subject of an EU adequacy decision, a valid transfer mechanism under GDPR Chapter V must be established for this data flow. The available options include:

> \(i\) Executing SCCs under Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914, likely Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor), with Stratosphere\'s Singapore operations designated as an additional data importer. Module 2 would be appropriate because the Singapore-based personnel are Processor employees accessing data on behalf of the Controller. Supplementary measures specific to the Singapore legal environment should be incorporated.
>
> \(ii\) Relying on derogations under GDPR Article 49. However, Article 49 derogations are interpreted narrowly and are generally not available for systematic or repetitive transfers. Because Singapore-based support engineers access EU data on a regular and ongoing basis for incident resolution, Article 49 derogations are unlikely to provide a sustainable legal basis.
>
> \(iii\) Implementing supplementary technical measures that limit the scope and nature of data accessible from Singapore, such as restricting Singapore-based personnel to anonymized or non-personal diagnostic data only, or restricting access to metadata without access to identifiable patient records.
>
> \(iv\) Alternatively, Stratosphere could restrict all access to EU personal data to personnel located within the EEA, thereby eliminating the need for a transfer mechanism for this scenario. This would require contractual commitment in the DPA and operational verification.

The current DPA Template\'s silence on this transfer constitutes a material compliance gap that must be resolved prior to DPA execution and the September 1, 2025 EU expansion launch date.

**[3.5 Diagram 5 --- EU Data to Orionis Analytics (Anonymization and Analytics)]{.underline}**

**Flow Description:**

This data flow involves the transfer of EU personal data from Stratosphere to Orionis Analytics Ltd. for anonymization and analytics processing. Both parties operate within the EEA.

**Source:** **Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH** --- Frankfurt Data Center (Germany) and/or Dublin Data Center (Ireland), acting as Processor.

**Transmission:** EU personal data is transferred to Orionis for anonymization and analytics processing. The DPA Template does not specify the encryption protocol or method for this specific intra-EEA transfer; counsel should confirm that appropriate technical measures are in place.

**Destination:** **Orionis Analytics Ltd.** --- Dublin, Ireland, acting as Subprocessor.

**Purpose:** Anonymization and analytics services as described in the DPA Template.

**Nature of Transfer:** This is an intra-EEA transfer from Germany/Ireland to Ireland. Both the data exporter (Stratosphere, Frankfurt/Dublin) and the data importer (Orionis, Dublin) are located within the European Economic Area. No GDPR Chapter V international transfer mechanism is required.

**FLAG FOR LEGAL REVIEW --- Anonymization vs. Pseudonymization :** Data sent to Orionis for \"anonymization\" is personal data at the point of transfer and must be protected accordingly under the GDPR. The critical question is whether Orionis\'s output constitutes truly anonymized data (which would fall outside the scope of the GDPR) or pseudonymized data (which remains personal data subject to the full panoply of GDPR obligations).

The DPA must be amended to address this issue comprehensively. Specifically, the DPA should:

> \(1\) Define the anonymization standard by reference to objective and verifiable criteria, including the three-criteria test established in WP29 Opinion 05/2014 (WP216): (a) singling out --- it should not be possible to isolate an individual from the dataset; (b) linkability --- it should not be possible to link records relating to the same individual across datasets; and (c) inference --- it should not be possible to deduce information about an individual from the data with significant probability.
>
> \(2\) Require Orionis to validate and certify that its outputs meet the defined anonymization standard, with such validation to be documented and made available to Pinnacle EU B.V. upon request.
>
> \(3\) Specify that if Orionis\'s outputs do not meet the defined anonymization standard, those outputs shall be treated as \"Personal Data\" under the DPA and shall remain subject to all DPA obligations, including security measures, data retention limits, data subject rights facilitation, breach notification, and, if transferred outside the EEA at any future point, international transfer mechanisms.
>
> \(4\) Address whether the analytics processing performed on data prior to the completion of the anonymization process constitutes a separate processing activity requiring its own documentation of lawful basis and purpose limitation under Articles 5(1)(b) and 6 GDPR.

**[Section 6: Observations and Flags for Legal Review]{.underline}**

This section provides a consolidated list of all issues identified through the data flow mapping exercise described in this document. Each issue is cross-referenced to the relevant DPA Template section, the data flow diagram(s) in which the issue was identified, and the internal issue tracking reference. These flags are intended for use by the legal team in preparing the compliance gap memorandum and DPA redline.

**1. International Transfer --- Wrong SCC Module (Critical)**

The Processor-to-Subprocessor transfer from Stratosphere (Frankfurt data center) to Larkfield (Northern Virginia data center) for disaster recovery and business continuity purposes requires **SCC Module 3 (Processor-to-Subprocessor)** under Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914. The DPA Template (Section 7) references and attaches only Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor), which is legally insufficient for this transfer scenario. Module 3 must be separately executed between Stratosphere (as Processor/data exporter) and Larkfield (as Subprocessor/data importer), with Pinnacle EU B.V. designated as the Controller with enforceable third-party beneficiary rights under the SCCs. Without the correct Module 3 SCCs in place, there is no valid legal mechanism for this transfer under GDPR Chapter V. *See Diagram 3 (Section 3.3) and Summary Table (Section 4), Transfer #2.*.

**2. International Transfer --- Singapore Remote Access Not Covered (High)**

Stratosphere support engineers based in Singapore access EU personal data stored at the Frankfurt and Dublin data centers on a regular basis for incident resolution and technical support. This remote access constitutes an international transfer under the GDPR. No transfer mechanism is specified, referenced, or contemplated in the DPA Template for this scenario. DPA Section 7 is entirely silent on Singapore. The DPA must include a valid GDPR Chapter V mechanism (most likely Module 2 SCCs with Singapore-specific supplementary measures) or Stratosphere must contractually commit to restricting EU data access to EEA-based personnel exclusively. *See Diagram 4 (Section 3.4) and Summary Table (Section 4), Transfer #3.* \[References: \]

**3. International Transfer --- Larkfield Not DPF-Certified (High)**

Larkfield Data Systems, LLC is not certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. The DPF adequacy decision (adopted July 10, 2023) cannot be relied upon as an alternative or supplementary transfer mechanism for any data flows involving Larkfield as the data importer. SCCs under Module 3, accompanied by supplementary measures and a Transfer Impact Assessment, are required. Pinnacle should also consider requesting that Larkfield obtain DPF certification prior to the September 1, 2025 go-live date as an additional protective measure. *See Section 1.3.1, Diagram 3 (Section 3.3), and Summary Table (Section 4), Transfer #2.* \[References: \]

**4. International Transfer --- No Transfer Impact Assessment (High)**

The DPA Template does not require, reference, or document any Transfer Impact Assessment for transfers to the United States (Transfer #2) or for remote access from Singapore (Transfer #3). Following the CJEU\'s *Schrems II* judgment (Case C-311/18) and EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 (Version 2.0), a TIA is a prerequisite for reliance on SCCs as a transfer mechanism. The TIA must assess US and Singaporean surveillance laws, the availability of effective legal remedies, and the necessity of supplementary measures. The DPA must require the completion and documentation of a TIA for each identified international transfer, with provisions for periodic reassessment as the legal landscape evolves. *See Diagram 3 (Section 3.3), Diagram 4 (Section 3.4), and Summary Table (Section 4).* \[References: \]

**5. Anonymization Standard Undefined (Medium-High)**

Orionis Analytics Ltd. provides \"anonymization and analytics\" services, but the DPA Template does not define anonymization or distinguish it from pseudonymization. If Orionis\'s outputs are pseudonymized rather than truly anonymized under the standard established in WP29 Opinion 05/2014 (WP216, endorsed by the EDPB), those outputs remain personal data under the GDPR and are subject to all DPA obligations. The DPA must: (a) define the anonymization standard by reference to the WP29/EDPB three-criteria test (singling out, linkability, inference); (b) require Orionis to validate and certify that its outputs satisfy the defined standard; (c) specify that outputs failing to meet the standard are treated as personal data subject to all DPA protections; and (d) address whether pre-anonymization analytics processing requires separate lawful basis documentation. *See Section 1.3.2, Diagram 5 (Section 3.5), and Summary Table (Section 4), Transfer #4.* \[References: \]

**[SECTION 4 --- CONFIDENTIALITY]{.underline}**

**4.1** The Processor shall ensure that all persons authorized to Process Personal Data on behalf of the Controller, including the Processor\'s employees, contractors, temporary workers, and agents, have committed themselves to confidentiality or are under an appropriate statutory obligation of confidentiality, in accordance with Article 28(3)(b) of the GDPR. The Processor shall maintain written records of such confidentiality commitments and shall make them available to the Controller upon request.

**4.2** The Processor shall ensure that access to Personal Data Processed on behalf of the Controller is strictly limited to those members of the Processor\'s personnel who require such access for the performance of the Services under the Agreement. The Processor shall implement appropriate access management procedures, including role-based access controls and least-privilege principles, to enforce this limitation. The Processor shall promptly revoke access for any personnel member whose role no longer requires access to the Controller\'s Personal Data.

**4.3** The obligations set forth in this Section 4 shall survive the termination or expiration of this DPA and shall continue in full force and effect for so long as the Processor or any of its personnel retains any Personal Data Processed on behalf of the Controller.

**4.4** The Processor shall not disclose Personal Data to any third party, including any governmental authority or body, except as expressly authorized by the Controller in writing, as required by applicable European Union or Member State law, or as otherwise permitted under this DPA (including disclosure to authorized Subprocessors in accordance with Section 6).

**[SECTION 5 --- SECURITY OF PROCESSING]{.underline}**

**5.1** The Processor shall implement and maintain appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk presented by the Processing, in accordance with Article 32 of the GDPR. In determining the appropriate level of security, the Processor shall take into account the state of the art, the costs of implementation, and the nature, scope, context, and purposes of Processing, as well as the risk of varying likelihood and severity for the rights and freedoms of the natural persons whose Personal Data is Processed. The Processor acknowledges that the Personal Data Processed under this DPA includes special categories of data (health data) and shall ensure that the security measures reflect the heightened sensitivity of such data.

**5.2** The technical and organizational measures implemented by the Processor are described in detail in Annex B (Technical and Organizational Measures) to this DPA, which forms an integral part of this DPA and is incorporated herein by reference. Without limiting the generality of Section 5.1, such measures include, as of the date of this DPA:

> \(a\) Encryption of Personal Data at rest using the Advanced Encryption Standard with 256-bit keys (AES-256) across all data storage systems and media utilized in the delivery of the Services;
>
> \(b\) Encryption of Personal Data in transit using Transport Layer Security version 1.3 (TLS 1.3) for all data transmissions between the Controller\'s systems and the Processor\'s infrastructure, as well as between the Processor\'s data centers and between the Processor and its Subprocessors;
>
> \(c\) Logical access controls, including role-based access control (RBAC) with least-privilege principles, multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all administrative and privileged access, and segregation of duties for critical Processing activities;
>
> \(d\) Annual penetration testing conducted by an independent third-party information security firm, with findings reported to the Processor\'s Chief Information Security Officer and remediation tracked to completion;
>
> \(e\) Intrusion detection and prevention systems (IDS/IPS) deployed across all network segments and monitored on a continuous 24/7 basis by the Processor\'s security operations center;
>
> \(f\) Regular vulnerability scanning conducted on a monthly basis, with critical and high-severity vulnerabilities remediated within timeframes established by the Processor\'s vulnerability management policy, and a formalized patch management program.

**5.3** The Processor shall regularly test, assess, and evaluate the effectiveness of its technical and organizational measures for ensuring the security of Processing, in accordance with Article 32(1)(d) of the GDPR. **[SECTION 9 --- PERSONAL DATA BREACH NOTIFICATION]{.underline}**

**9.1** The Processor shall notify the Controller of any Personal Data Breach without undue delay and in any event no later than forty-eight (48) hours after becoming aware of the Personal Data Breach. For the purposes of this Section 9, the Processor shall be deemed to have become \"aware\" of a Personal Data Breach when the Processor\'s incident response team or any member of the Processor\'s management has confirmed, following initial assessment, that a security incident constitutes a Personal Data Breach within the meaning of Article 4(12) of the GDPR. The Processor shall maintain documented procedures to ensure that potential Personal Data Breaches are identified, escalated, and assessed promptly.

**9.2** The notification provided under Section 9.1 shall include, to the extent such information is available at the time of notification and to the extent it can be provided without unreasonable delay:

> \(a\) A description of the nature of the Personal Data Breach, including, where possible, the categories and approximate number of Data Subjects concerned and the categories and approximate number of Personal Data records concerned;
>
> \(b\) The name and contact details of the Processor\'s Data Protection Officer (or, if the Data Protection Officer is unavailable, another designated contact point) where more information can be obtained regarding the Personal Data Breach;
>
> \(c\) A description of the likely consequences of the Personal Data Breach, including an assessment of the potential risks to the rights and freedoms of affected Data Subjects;
>
> \(d\) A description of the measures taken or proposed to be taken by the Processor to address the Personal Data Breach, including, where appropriate, measures to contain the breach, mitigate its possible adverse effects, and prevent recurrence.

**9.3** Where, and to the extent that, it is not possible to provide all of the information specified in Section 9.2 at the same time as the initial notification, the Processor shall provide such information in phases without undue further delay as additional information becomes available. The Processor shall provide supplemental notifications to the Controller as soon as reasonably practicable and in any event shall endeavor to provide complete information within seventy-two (72) hours of the initial notification.

**9.4** The Processor shall document all Personal Data Breaches, including the facts relating to the Personal Data Breach, its effects, and the remedial action taken, in accordance with Article 33(5) of the GDPR. Such documentation shall be maintained for a period of not less than three (3) years from the date of the Personal Data Breach and shall be made available to the Controller upon request.

**9.5** The Processor shall cooperate with and assist the Controller in the Controller\'s performance of its obligations under Articles 33 and 34 of the GDPR, including the Controller\'s obligation to notify the competent Supervisory Authority and, where applicable, to communicate the Personal Data Breach to affected Data Subjects. The Processor shall provide such cooperation and assistance promptly and in a manner that enables the Controller to meet the applicable notification timelines under the GDPR.

**9.6** In the event that the Processor fails to provide the initial notification of a Personal Data Breach within the forty-eight (48) hour timeline specified in Section 9.1, the Processor shall pay to the Controller a penalty of one thousand Euros (€1,000) per calendar day of delay commencing on the date that is forty-eight (48) hours after the Processor became aware of the Personal Data Breach and continuing until the date on which notification is actually provided to the Controller, provided that such penalty shall not exceed fifty thousand Euros (€50,000) in the aggregate per breach incident. The Parties acknowledge that such penalties represent a genuine pre-estimate of the Controller\'s loss resulting from delayed notification and are not intended as punitive damages.

**9.7** The obligations set forth in this Section 9 are without prejudice to any other rights, remedies, or claims the Controller may have under this DPA, the Agreement, or applicable law in connection with a Personal Data Breach.
