**[ANNEX B --- TECHNICAL AND ORGANIZATIONAL MEASURES]{.underline}**

This Annex B forms an integral part of the Data Processing Agreement (\"DPA\") and describes the technical and organizational measures implemented by the Processor to ensure the security and protection of Personal Data Processed on behalf of the Controller. These measures are designed to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, in accordance with Article 32 of the GDPR, and are subject to ongoing review and improvement.

**B.1 Encryption. Encryption at Rest:** All Personal Data stored in the Processor\'s data centers, including data stored in databases, file systems, object storage, and backup media, is encrypted at rest using the Advanced Encryption Standard with 256-bit keys (AES-256). Encryption at rest is applied uniformly across all storage tiers and replication targets, including primary storage in Frankfurt, secondary storage in Dublin, and disaster recovery storage in Northern Virginia.

**Encryption in Transit:** All data transmissions involving Personal Data are encrypted in transit using Transport Layer Security version 1.3 (TLS 1.3) or higher. This includes transmissions between the Controller\'s systems and the Processor\'s cloud infrastructure, transmissions between the Processor\'s data centers (Frankfurt, Dublin, and Northern Virginia), and transmissions between the Processor and its Subprocessors. The Processor does not support deprecated encryption protocols (including SSL 3.0, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1) for any connections involving Personal Data.

**Key Management:** Encryption keys are managed through a centralized key management system utilizing FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware security modules (HSMs). Encryption keys are generated using cryptographically secure random number generators, stored in the HSMs, and rotated on an annual basis in accordance with the Processor\'s key rotation policy. Key access is restricted to authorized personnel on a strict need-to-know basis, with all key management operations logged and auditable.

**B.2 Access Controls**

**Role-Based Access Control (RBAC):** The Processor implements role-based access control with least-privilege principles for all systems that Process Personal Data. Access to Personal Data is granted only to those personnel whose roles require such access for the performance of the Services, and access privileges are limited to the minimum level necessary for the performance of the assigned role.

**Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA):** Multi-factor authentication is required for all administrative and privileged access to systems that Process Personal Data. MFA is enforced through hardware tokens or authenticator applications; SMS-based authentication is not permitted for privileged access.

**Segregation of Duties:** Critical Processing activities, including database administration, key management, and access provisioning, are subject to segregation of duties controls. No single individual has the ability to perform all steps of a critical operation without independent verification or approval.

**Access Reviews:** The Processor\'s information security team conducts formal access reviews on a quarterly basis to verify that access privileges remain appropriate and aligned with current role assignments. Access that is no longer required is promptly revoked. Access review results are documented and retained for a minimum of three (3) years.

**B.3 Network Security**

**Firewalls and Network Segmentation:** The Processor\'s data centers employ multi-layered firewall architectures with network segmentation between client environments, management networks, and public-facing services. Each client environment is logically isolated from other client environments and from the Processor\'s internal management infrastructure.

**Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS):** The Processor deploys intrusion detection and prevention systems across all network segments. IDS/IPS systems are monitored continuously (24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year) by the Processor\'s security operations center (SOC). Alerts are triaged and escalated in accordance with the Processor\'s incident response procedures.

**Vulnerability Scanning and Penetration Testing:** Automated vulnerability scanning is performed on a monthly basis across all systems and network segments that Process Personal Data. Critical and high-severity vulnerabilities are remediated within fourteen (14) calendar days of identification; medium-severity vulnerabilities are remediated within thirty (30) calendar days. Annual penetration testing is conducted by an independent, qualified third-party information security firm. Penetration test findings are reported to the Processor\'s Chief Information Security Officer and tracked to remediation.

**DDoS Mitigation:** The Processor employs distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) mitigation services to protect its cloud infrastructure and the Controller\'s hosted applications from volumetric, protocol, and application-layer DDoS attacks.

**B.4 Physical Security**

**Data Center Security:** All data centers utilized by the Processor (including subprocessor-operated data centers in Dublin and Northern Virginia) are equipped with the following physical security controls:

> • 24/7 on-site security personnel
>
> • Closed-circuit television (CCTV) surveillance with a minimum of ninety (90) days of recorded footage retention
>
> • Biometric access controls (fingerprint or iris scan) at all entry points to data processing areas
>
> • Mantrap (airlock) entry systems at primary data center entrances
>
> • Visitor management procedures requiring escort by authorized personnel at all times

**Environmental Controls:** Data centers are equipped with:

> • Fire detection and suppression systems (pre-action dry pipe sprinkler systems and gas-based suppression for server rooms)
>
> • Climate control systems maintaining optimal temperature and humidity for computing equipment
>
> • Redundant power supply, including uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems and on-site diesel generators with a minimum of seventy-two (72) hours of fuel reserve
>
> • Redundant network connectivity from multiple independent telecommunications providers

**B.6 Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery**

**Geographic Redundancy:** Personal Data is replicated across geographically redundant data centers (Frankfurt, Dublin, and Northern Virginia) to ensure availability and resilience in the event of a localized outage, natural disaster, or other disruption affecting a single data center.

**Recovery Point Objective (RPO):** The Processor maintains a recovery point objective of one (1) hour, meaning that in the event of a disaster or system failure, the maximum data loss shall not exceed one (1) hour of data.

**Recovery Time Objective (RTO):** The Processor maintains a recovery time objective of four (4) hours, meaning that in the event of a disaster or system failure affecting the primary production environment, the Processor targets restoration of Services within four (4) hours.

**Disaster Recovery Testing:** The Processor conducts comprehensive disaster recovery testing at least once per year, including simulated failover to the Northern Virginia disaster recovery site. Test results are documented and reviewed by the Processor\'s Chief Information Security Officer and Chief Technology Officer.

**B.7 Personnel Security**

**Background Checks:** All Processor personnel who have access to Personal Data are subject to background checks prior to commencing employment or engagement, including verification of identity, criminal records checks (to the extent permitted by applicable law), and verification of professional qualifications where relevant.

**Confidentiality Agreements:** All Processor personnel with access to Personal Data are required to execute written confidentiality agreements in accordance with Section 4 of the DPA.

**Security Awareness Training:** All Processor personnel receive annual security awareness training covering topics including data protection principles, information security policies and procedures, social engineering and phishing awareness, incident reporting procedures, and secure data handling practices. Training completion records are maintained by the Processor\'s human resources department.

**B.8 Incident Response**

**Incident Response Plan:** The Processor maintains a documented incident response plan that is reviewed and updated at least annually. The incident response plan addresses the identification, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident review of security incidents, including Personal Data Breaches.

**Incident Response Team:** The Processor maintains a designated incident response team that is available twenty-four (24) hours a day, seven (7) days a week, three hundred sixty-five (365) days a year. The incident response team includes representatives from information security, legal, operations, and communications functions.

**Alignment with ISO 27001:** The Processor\'s incident response procedures are aligned with the requirements of ISO/IEC 27001:2022, specifically Annex A Control A.5.24 (Information security incident management planning and preparation), A.5.25 (Assessment and decision on information security events), A.5.26 (Response to information security incidents), and A.5.27 (Learning from information security incidents).

**B.9 Certifications and Audits**

**ISO 27001:2022 Certification:** The Processor holds ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification, Certificate Number ISO-27001-SC-2024-0891, issued by TÜV Rheinland AG on June 15, 2024, valid through June 14, 2027. The certification covers the Processor\'s information security management system as it applies to the provision of cloud hosting, managed database, and analytics services from the Processor\'s Frankfurt data center.

**SOC 2 Type II Report:** The Processor obtains an annual SOC 2 Type II report covering the Trust Services Criteria (Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy). The most recent SOC 2 Type II report was dated September 30, 2024, covering the audit period from October 1, 2023 through September 30, 2024, and was issued by Clearwater Audit Partners GmbH. The SOC 2 Type II report is available to the Controller upon request, subject to the execution of a non-disclosure agreement where required by the Processor\'s auditor.

**Ongoing Compliance:** The Processor is committed to maintaining its ISO 27001 certification and obtaining annual SOC 2 Type II reports throughout the term of the DPA. The Processor shall promptly notify the Controller of any material findings, qualifications, or exceptions identified in any certification audit or SOC 2 examination that are relevant to the Processing of Personal Data on behalf of the Controller.

*End of Annex B --- Technical and Organizational Measures*

35: **[Section 1: Purpose and Scope of This Playbook]{.underline}**
36: 
37: This playbook sets forth Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc.\'s (\"**Pinnacle**\" or the \"**Company**\") mandatory, preferred, and fallback negotiation positions for Data Processing Agreements (\"**DPAs**\") with third-party vendors and service providers that process personal data on Pinnacle\'s behalf. The purpose of this document is to ensure consistency, regulatory compliance, and efficient negotiation across all vendor DPA engagements by providing Pinnacle\'s legal team and authorized negotiators with clear, tiered guidance on acceptable contractual terms.
38: 
39: Pinnacle is a Delaware corporation operating as a US-based digital health platform company. The Company provides cloud-based electronic health records management, telehealth facilitation, patient engagement tools, and healthcare analytics services to healthcare providers across the United States.
40: 
41: Pinnacle acts as a **HIPAA Covered Entity** for certain data flows involving Protected Health Information (\"**PHI**\") of approximately **2.1 million US patients** and approximately **14,000 US healthcare provider contacts**. These data flows are central to Pinnacle\'s core service offerings and are implicated in the majority of vendor engagements involving clinical and patient-facing data processing activities.
42: 
43: Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately **890,000 California residents**, triggering obligations under the California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (\"**CCPA/CPRA**\"). Given the significant volume of California resident data processed by Pinnacle and its vendors, CCPA/CPRA compliance is a primary concern in all vendor DPA negotiations involving consumer-facing data.
44: 
45: Pinnacle is expanding into the European Union with a target launch date of **September 1, 2025**. The Company\'s EU operations will be conducted through its wholly owned subsidiary, **Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.**, registered in the Netherlands at Herengracht 450, 1017 CA Amsterdam. Pinnacle EU B.V. will act as Controller under the General Data Protection Regulation (\"**GDPR**\") for an estimated **150,000 projected EU patients** and approximately **320 EU healthcare provider contacts** in Year 1. This EU expansion introduces GDPR obligations that intersect with and complement Pinnacle\'s existing US data protection requirements.
46: 
47: This playbook addresses the following regulatory regimes and their implications for vendor DPA negotiations:
48: 
49: > • **HIPAA/HITECH**, including Business Associate Agreement (\"BAA\") requirements;
50: >
51: > • **CCPA/CPRA**, including Service Provider qualification and certification requirements;
52: >
53: > • **GDPR**, including Article 28 processor requirements and cross-border data transfer mechanisms; and
54: >
55: > • **Pinnacle\'s internal data governance standards**, which in certain areas exceed the minimum requirements of applicable law.
56: 
57: **Important Note:** This playbook does NOT replace the requirement for outside counsel review of DPAs involving novel or high-risk processing activities. Negotiators must escalate to **Rachel Osterfeld** at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP for matters involving cross-border transfers to jurisdictions without adequacy decisions, novel HIPAA scenarios (including first-of-kind technology deployments involving PHI), regulatory enforcement actions or investigations, or any matter where the vendor\'s proposed terms deviate materially from the positions set forth herein and the applicable fallback position is inadequate to protect Pinnacle\'s interests.
58: 
59: **[Section 2: Regulatory Framework Overview]{.underline}**
60: 
61: Pinnacle\'s vendor DPA negotiations must account for three primary regulatory regimes, each of which imposes distinct and, in some cases, overlapping requirements on the contractual relationship between Pinnacle and its data processing vendors. Understanding the interplay among these regimes is essential for effective negotiation. This Section provides a summary overview; detailed negotiation positions for each regime are set forth in the Sections that follow.
62: 
63: The three regimes are: (1) the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, as amended by the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act of 2009 (\"**HIPAA/HITECH**\"); (2) the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020 (\"**CCPA/CPRA**\"); and (3) the General Data Protection Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (\"**GDPR**\"). Each regime imposes its own definitions, obligations, and enforcement mechanisms, and each requires specific contractual provisions in vendor agreements. Where a vendor processes data subject to multiple regimes (which is increasingly common in Pinnacle\'s vendor portfolio), the DPA must address all applicable requirements, and the most restrictive standard generally governs.
64: 
65: Negotiators should be aware that many vendor-provided DPA templates are drafted primarily with GDPR in mind and may fail to address HIPAA or CCPA/CPRA requirements. It is the negotiator\'s responsibility to identify these gaps and require the addition of all necessary provisions before execution.
66: 
67: **[2.1 HIPAA / HITECH]{.underline}**
68: 
69: Pinnacle is a **Covered Entity** under HIPAA as defined in 45 CFR § 160.103. Any vendor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits Protected Health Information (\"**PHI**\") on Pinnacle\'s behalf qualifies as a **Business Associate** under 45 CFR § 160.103 and is subject to the full range of HIPAA and HITECH requirements applicable to Business Associates.
70: 
71: All DPAs with Business Associates **MUST** incorporate a **Business Associate Agreement** (\"**BAA**\"), either as an integrated section within the DPA body or as a standalone exhibit appended to and expressly incorporated by reference into the DPA. This requirement is non-negotiable and derives from the mandatory contractual provisions set forth in **45 CFR § 164.502(e)** and **45 CFR § 164.504(e)**.
72: 
73: A compliant BAA must include, at a minimum, the following elements:
74: 
75: 1\. **Definitions** of PHI, Covered Entity, and Business Associate consistent with HIPAA regulatory definitions;
76: 
77: 2\. **Permitted uses and disclosures** of PHI, limited to those necessary to perform services under the DPA and Master Services Agreement (\"MSA\"), and consistent with the minimum necessary standard;
78: 
79: 3\. **Minimum necessary standard** compliance (45 CFR § 164.502(b)), requiring the vendor to limit its use, disclosure, and requests for PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of the processing;
80: 
81: 4\. **Workforce training requirements**, obligating the vendor to train all workforce members with access to PHI on HIPAA privacy and security requirements;
82: 
83: 5\. **Breach notification obligations**, requiring prompt notification to Pinnacle, and supporting Pinnacle\'s obligations to notify affected individuals and the Department of Health and Human Services (\"**HHS**\") in accordance with the HITECH Act breach notification provisions;
84: 
85: 6\. **HIPAA Security Rule safeguard categories**, requiring the vendor to implement and maintain reasonable and appropriate administrative safeguards (45 CFR § 164.308), physical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.310), and technical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.312);
86: 
87: 7\. **Subcontractor flow-down of BAA terms**, requiring the vendor to ensure that any subcontractor or agent that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on vendor\'s behalf agrees to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements that apply to the vendor under the BAA (45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii));
88: 
89: 8\. **Record retention of six (6) years** per 45 CFR § 164.530(j), covering all HIPAA-required documentation including the BAA itself, policies and procedures, training records, and incident records; and
90: 
91: 9\. **Return or destruction of PHI at termination**, with exceptions where return or destruction is infeasible, in which case the protections of the BAA must extend to all retained PHI for as long as it is maintained.
92: 
93: Negotiators should be particularly alert to vendor DPA templates that reference GDPR Article 28 processor requirements but omit any reference to HIPAA. Where a vendor will process PHI, the absence of a BAA renders the DPA non-compliant regardless of how robust the GDPR provisions may be.
94: 
95: **[2.2 CCPA / CPRA]{.underline}**
96: 
97: Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately **890,000 California residents** across its patient-facing platform, provider network, and marketing and analytics activities. This volume substantially exceeds the CCPA/CPRA applicability thresholds and places Pinnacle squarely within the statute\'s scope as a \"**Business**\" under Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(d).
98: 
99: Vendors that process California personal information on Pinnacle\'s behalf must qualify as \"**Service Providers**\" under Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ag). The Service Provider designation is not automatic; it requires specific contractual provisions that restrict the vendor\'s use, retention, and disclosure of personal information received from Pinnacle. Without these contractual provisions, a vendor may be deemed a \"third party\" under the CCPA/CPRA, which could expose Pinnacle to claims that it has \"sold\" or \"shared\" personal information in violation of the statute.
100: 
101: DPAs with vendors processing California personal information must include the following provisions, which are treated as **must-have** requirements in all negotiations:
102: 
103: > • A **contractual prohibition** on selling or sharing personal information, as those terms are defined in Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ad) (\"sale\") and § 1798.140(ah) (\"share\");
104: >
105: > • A **prohibition on combining** personal information received from Pinnacle with personal information received from any other person or entity, or collected from the consumer\'s own direct interaction with the vendor, except as expressly permitted by the CCPA/CPRA;
106: >
107: > • A **prohibition on using** personal information for any purpose other than the specific business purpose set forth in the DPA or MSA, including any commercial purpose other than providing the services specified in the agreement;
108: >
109: > • A **certification** in which the vendor expressly certifies that it understands these restrictions and will comply with them, as required under CPRA amendments to Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(d).
110: 
111: These provisions are mandatory for all vendors with access to California resident data. A vendor DPA that omits these provisions, or that contains language inconsistent with the Service Provider classification, must be redlined before execution. Detailed negotiation positions for CCPA/CPRA terms are set forth in Section 7 of this playbook.
112: 
113: **[2.3 GDPR]{.underline}**
114: 
115: Upon Pinnacle\'s EU expansion, which is scheduled for **September 1, 2025**, Pinnacle (acting through its subsidiary **Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.**) will function as **Controller** under the GDPR for the processing of personal data of EU/EEA data subjects. Vendor DPAs must comply with **GDPR Article 28** processor requirements, which mandate a written contract between the controller and processor that sets forth the subject-matter and duration of processing, the nature and purpose of processing, the types of personal data and categories of data subjects, and the obligations and rights of the controller.
116: 
117: Where personal data is transferred outside the European Economic Area (\"**EEA**\"), appropriate transfer mechanisms must be in place. Acceptable mechanisms include:
118: 
119: > • **EU Standard Contractual Clauses (\"SCCs\")** per Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914, with the appropriate module selected for each transfer relationship;
120: >
121: > • **EU-US Data Privacy Framework** certification, where the receiving entity is certified and the certification covers the relevant data processing activities; and
122: >
123: > • **Binding Corporate Rules**, where applicable and approved by the competent supervisory authority.
124: 
125: GDPR requirements are addressed in this playbook where they intersect with US negotiation positions, particularly with respect to cross-border data transfers, breach notification, data subject rights, and subprocessor obligations. A separate **EU DPA Addendum Checklist** is maintained by outside counsel at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP and should be consulted for all DPAs involving EU data processing. Negotiators working on DPAs with a GDPR component should coordinate with outside counsel to ensure that the EU-specific requirements are fully addressed.
126: 
127: **[Section 3: Definitions --- Required Contractual Definitions]{.underline}**
128: 
129: Every Pinnacle DPA must include clearly defined terms organized by regulatory regime. The inclusion of complete and accurate definitions is essential to ensuring that the DPA\'s operative provisions are enforceable and that each party\'s obligations are unambiguous. This Section sets forth the required defined terms and Pinnacle\'s negotiation positions regarding their inclusion.
130: 
131: **[3.1 Required Defined Terms by Regulatory Regime]{.underline}**
132: 
133: **GDPR Definitions (per Article 4)**
134: 
135: The following terms must be defined consistently with GDPR Article 4:
136: 
137: > • **Personal Data** (Art. 4(1))
138: >
139: > • **Processing** (Art. 4(2))
140: >
141: > • **Controller** (Art. 4(7))
142: >
143: > • **Processor** (Art. 4(8))
144: >
145: > • **Data Subject** (Art. 4(1))
146: >
147: > • **Personal Data Breach** (Art. 4(12))
148: >
149: > • **Supervisory Authority** (Art. 4(21))
150: 
151: **HIPAA Definitions (per 45 CFR § 160.103 and the HITECH Act)**
152: 
153: The following terms must be defined consistently with HIPAA regulatory definitions:
154: 
155: > • **Protected Health Information (PHI)** (45 CFR § 160.103)
156: >
157: > • **Electronic Protected Health Information (ePHI)** (45 CFR § 160.103)
158: >
159: > • **Covered Entity** (45 CFR § 160.103)
160: >
161: > • **Business Associate** (45 CFR § 160.103)
162: >
163: > • **Business Associate Agreement** (45 CFR § 164.504(e))
164: >
165: > • **Breach** (as defined under the HITECH Act, 42 U.S.C. § 17921(1))
166: >
167: > • **Unsecured PHI** (45 CFR § 164.402)
168: 
169: **CCPA/CPRA Definitions (per Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140)**
170: 
171: The following terms must be defined consistently with the CCPA/CPRA statutory definitions:
172: 
173: > • **Personal Information** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(v))
174: >
175: > • **Service Provider** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ag))
176: >
177: > • **Business** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(d))
178: >
179: > • **Business Purpose** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(e))
180: >
181: > • **Sale** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ad))
182: >
183: > • **Share** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(ah))
184: >
185: > • **Consumer** (Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.140(i))
186: 
187: **[3.2 Negotiation Positions for Definitions]{.underline}**
188: 
189: **Must-have:** The DPA must include all three sets of definitions where the vendor processes data subject to multiple regulatory regimes. Many vendor-provided DPA templates are drafted to address GDPR only and will include GDPR definitions but omit HIPAA and CCPA/CPRA definitions entirely. Where this is the case, the negotiator must require the addition of both the HIPAA definitions and the CCPA/CPRA definitions before the DPA is finalized. A DPA that covers PHI but lacks the defined term \"Protected Health Information\" creates ambiguity regarding the scope of the vendor\'s obligations and may be insufficient to satisfy the BAA requirements of 45 CFR § 164.504(e). 191: **Nice-to-have:** A single, integrated definitions section within the DPA body, rather than separate definitions scattered across the DPA, BAA exhibit, and CCPA addendum. 196: 
197: This Section addresses the most critical requirement for US healthcare vendor DPAs: the **HIPAA Business Associate Agreement**. The BAA is not a discretionary contract term; it is a **regulatory mandate** under 45 CFR § 164.502(e) and 45 CFR § 164.504(e). 201: **[4.1 BAA as Must-Have]{.underline}**

203: **Must-have:** The vendor DPA must include a fully compliant HIPAA BAA, either integrated into the DPA body or attached as a standalone exhibit that is expressly incorporated by reference into the DPA. No DPA may be executed without a BAA where the vendor processes PHI.

207: > **(a) Permitted Uses and Disclosures.** Vendor\'s uses and disclosures of PHI must be limited to those necessary to perform the services described in the DPA and the applicable MSA, and must be consistent with Pinnacle\'s minimum necessary policies. 216: >

218: >
219: > \(iii\) **Technical safeguards** per 45 CFR § 164.312, including access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, person or entity authentication, and transmission security.
220: >
221: > **(e) Subcontractor Flow-Down.** Vendor must ensure that any subcontractor or agent that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on behalf of vendor agrees to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements that apply to vendor under the BAA, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii). 224: >
225: > **(g) Record Retention.** Vendor must retain HIPAA-required documentation for a period of six (6) years from the date of creation or the date when the document was last in effect, whichever is later, in accordance with 45 CFR § 164.530(j). 227: > **(h) Return or Destruction of PHI at Termination.** Upon termination or expiration of the DPA/MSA, vendor must return or destroy all PHI in its possession, including all copies in any form or medium. Where return or destruction is infeasible (e.g., because PHI is embedded in archived backup systems), vendor must extend the protections of the BAA to all retained PHI and limit further uses and disclosures to those purposes that make return or destruction infeasible. Vendor must certify in writing that it has returned or destroyed all PHI, or that return or destruction is infeasible and identifying the specific PHI retained.

**[Section 1: Purpose and Scope of This Playbook]{.underline}**

This playbook sets forth Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc.\'s (\"**Pinnacle**\" or the \"**Company**\") mandatory, preferred, and fallback negotiation positions for Data Processing Agreements (\"**DPAs**\") with third-party vendors and service providers that process personal data on Pinnacle\'s behalf. The purpose of this document is to ensure consistency, regulatory compliance, and efficient negotiation across all vendor DPA engagements by providing Pinnacle\'s legal team and authorized negotiators with clear, tiered guidance on acceptable contractual terms.

Pinnacle is a Delaware corporation operating as a US-based digital health platform company. The Company provides cloud-based electronic health records management, telehealth facilitation, patient engagement tools, and healthcare analytics services to healthcare providers across the United States.

Pinnacle acts as a **HIPAA Covered Entity** for certain data flows involving Protected Health Information (\"**PHI**\") of approximately **2.1 million US patients** and approximately **14,000 US healthcare provider contacts**. These data flows are central to Pinnacle\'s core service offerings and are implicated in the majority of vendor engagements involving clinical and patient-facing data processing activities.

Pinnacle processes personal information of approximately **890,000 California residents**, triggering obligations under the California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (\"**CCPA/CPRA**\"). Given the significant volume of California resident data processed by Pinnacle and its vendors, CCPA/CPRA compliance is a primary concern in all vendor DPA negotiations involving consumer-facing data.

Pinnacle is expanding into the European Union with a target launch date of **September 1, 2025**. The Company\'s EU operations will be conducted through its wholly owned subsidiary, **Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.**, registered in the Netherlands at Herengracht 450, 1017 CA Amsterdam. Pinnacle EU B.V. will act as Controller under the General Data Protection Regulation (\"**GDPR**\") for an estimated **150,000 projected EU patients** and approximately **320 EU healthcare provider contacts** in Year 1. This EU expansion introduces GDPR obligations that intersect with and complement Pinnacle\'s existing US data protection requirements.
This playbook addresses the following regulatory regimes and their implications for vendor DPA negotiations:
> • **HIPAA/HITECH**, including Business Associate Agreement (\"BAA\") requirements;
> • **CCPA/CPRA**, including Service Provider qualification and certification requirements;
> • **GDPR**, including Article 28 processor requirements and cross-border data transfer mechanisms; and
> • **Pinnacle\'s internal data governance standards**, which in certain areas exceed the minimum requirements of applicable law.

**Important Note:** This playbook does NOT replace the requirement for outside counsel review of DPAs involving novel or high-risk processing activities. Negotiators must escalate to **Rachel Osterfeld** at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP for matters involving cross-border transfers to jurisdictions without adequacy decisions, novel HIPAA scenarios (including first-of-kind technology deployments involving PHI), regulatory enforcement actions or investigations, or any matter where the vendor\'s proposed terms deviate materially from the positions set forth herein and the applicable fallback position is inadequate to protect Pinnacle\'s interests.
**[Section 2: Regulatory Framework Overview]{.underline}**

Pinnacle\'s vendor DPA negotiations must account for three primary regulatory regimes, each of which imposes distinct and, in some cases, overlapping requirements on the contractual relationship between Pinnacle and its data processing vendors. Understanding the interplay among these regimes is essential for effective negotiation. This Section provides a summary overview; detailed negotiation positions for each regime are set forth in the Sections that follow.

The three regimes are: (1) the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, as amended by the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act of 2009 (\"**HIPAA/HITECH**\"); (2) the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020 (\"**CCPA/CPRA**\"); and (3) the General Data Protection Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (\"**GDPR**\"). Each regime imposes its own definitions, obligations, and enforcement mechanisms, and each requires specific contractual provisions in vendor agreements. Where a vendor processes data subject to multiple regimes (which is increasingly common in Pinnacle\'s vendor portfolio), the DPA must address all applicable requirements, and the most restrictive standard generally governs.

Negotiators should be aware that many vendor-provided DPA templates are drafted primarily with GDPR in mind and may fail to address HIPAA or CCPA/CPRA requirements. It is the negotiator\'s responsibility to identify these gaps and require the addition of all necessary provisions before execution.
**[2.1 HIPAA / HITECH]{.underline}**

Pinnacle is a **Covered Entity** under HIPAA as defined in 45 CFR § 160.103. Any vendor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits Protected Health Information (\"**PHI**\") on Pinnacle\'s behalf qualifies as a **Business Associate** under 45 CFR § 160.103 and is subject to the full range of HIPAA and HITECH requirements applicable to Business Associates.

All DPAs with Business Associates **MUST** incorporate a **Business Associate Agreement** (\"**BAA**\"), either as an integrated section within the DPA body or as a standalone exhibit appended to and expressly incorporated by reference into the DPA. This requirement is non-negotiable and derives from the mandatory contractual provisions set forth in **45 CFR § 164.502(e)** and **45 CFR § 164.504(e)**.
A compliant BAA must include, at a minimum, the following elements:
1\. **Definitions** of PHI, Covered Entity, and Business Associate consistent with HIPAA regulatory definitions;

2\. **Permitted uses and disclosures** of PHI, limited to those necessary to perform services under the DPA and Master Services Agreement (\"MSA\"), and consistent with the minimum necessary standard;

3\. **Minimum necessary standard** compliance (45 CFR § 164.502(b)), requiring the vendor to limit its use, disclosure, and requests for PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of the processing;

6\. **HIPAA Security Rule safeguard categories**, requiring the vendor to implement and maintain reasonable and appropriate administrative safeguards (45 CFR § 164.308), physical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.310), and technical safeguards (45 CFR § 164.312);

7\. **Subcontractor flow-down of BAA terms**, requiring the vendor to ensure that any subcontractor or agent that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on vendor\'s behalf agrees to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements that apply to the vendor under the BAA (45 CFR § 164.502(e)(1)(ii));

**[2.3 GDPR]{.underline}**

Vendor DPAs must comply with **GDPR Article 28** processor requirements, which mandate a written contract between the controller and processor that sets forth the subject-matter and duration of processing, the nature and purpose of processing, the types of personal data and categories of data subjects, and the obligations and rights of the controller.
Where personal data is transferred outside the European Economic Area (\"**EEA**\"), appropriate transfer mechanisms must be in place. Acceptable mechanisms include:
> • **EU Standard Contractual Clauses (\"SCCs\")** per Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914, with the appropriate module selected for each transfer relationship;
> • **EU-US Data Privacy Framework** certification, where the receiving entity is certified and the certification covers the relevant data processing activities; and
> • **Binding Corporate Rules**, where applicable and approved by the competent supervisory authority.

GDPR requirements are addressed in this playbook where they intersect with US negotiation positions, particularly with respect to cross-border data transfers, breach notification, data subject rights, and subprocessor obligations. A separate **EU DPA Addendum Checklist** is maintained by outside counsel at Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP and should be consulted for all DPAs involving EU data processing. Negotiators working on DPAs with a GDPR component should coordinate with outside counsel to ensure that the EU-specific requirements are fully addressed.

**DPA Governing Law --- Separate Treatment:** The MSA acknowledges that the Data Processing Agreement may contain its own governing law and dispute resolution provisions, which shall govern data-protection-specific disputes to the extent expressly provided therein. *Note: The DPA template circulated by Stratosphere (Version 3.2, dated January 10, 2025) specifies the laws of the Federal Republic of Germany as the governing law for all DPA-related matters and provides for arbitration administered by the DIS (Deutsche Institution für Schiedsgerichtsbarkeit e.V. / German Institution of Arbitration) with the seat of arbitration in Munich, Germany, for all DPA-related disputes, including disputes involving the processing of US-origin data. This creates a potential three-way governing law framework: MSA disputes (New York law / AAA, New York); DPA disputes as currently proposed by Stratosphere (German law / DIS, Munich); and Pinnacle\'s internal legal playbook preference for US-specific data processing disputes (Delaware law / US District Court, Western District of Texas, Austin Division). This complexity is noted for purposes of the ongoing DPA negotiation.*
**[Section 9 --- Data Processing Agreement]{.underline}**

**DPA Requirement:** The MSA contemplates that a Data Processing Agreement (\"DPA\") shall be negotiated, finalized, and executed as Exhibit D to the MSA prior to the commencement of any processing of personal data by Stratosphere (or any of its authorized subprocessors) on behalf of Pinnacle or Pinnacle EU under the MSA.

**DPA as Condition Precedent to EU Launch:** The execution of a fully conforming DPA is a condition precedent to the commencement of EU Services under the MSA. The targeted EU Go-Live Date is September 1, 2025.

**Current Status of DPA Negotiation:** Stratosphere circulated its standard DPA template (Version 3.2, dated January 10, 2025) to Pinnacle on April 14, 2025. Pinnacle\'s internal review of the DPA template is targeted for completion by May 16, 2025. The DPA is currently under active review by Pinnacle\'s Office of General Counsel and by Pinnacle\'s outside counsel, Alderton Shaw & Whitmore LLP, with offices at 900 K Street NW, Suite 700, Washington, DC 20001 (lead partner for this engagement: Rachel Osterfeld).

**Scope of the DPA:** The DPA will cover all processing of personal data by Stratosphere and its authorized subprocessors --- specifically, Larkfield Data Systems, LLC and Orionis Analytics Ltd. --- on behalf of Pinnacle under the MSA, encompassing both US and EU data processing activities across all data center locations and all support access points (including remote access by Singapore-based support engineers).

**Regulatory Framework:** The DPA must address and ensure compliance with the EU General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) (\"GDPR\"), the US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, as amended (\"HIPAA\"), the California Consumer Privacy Act as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (\"CCPA/CPRA\"), and any other data protection, privacy, or information security laws applicable to the processing activities contemplated under the MSA.
**Stratosphere\'s Outside Counsel for DPA Negotiation:** Voss Kellner Rechtsanwälte, Maximilianstraße 35, 80539 Munich, Germany (lead partner: Dr. Karin Beckert).
**Stratosphere Data Protection Officer:** Dr. Annika Vogt, Data Protection Officer, Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH (contact: dpo@stratospherecloud.example.com).
**[Section 10 --- Certifications and Compliance]{.underline}**
Stratosphere currently holds the following certifications relevant to the services provided under the MSA:

> \(a\) **ISO/IEC 27001:2022** --- Information Security Management Systems. Certificate No. ISO-27001-SC-2024-0891, issued by TÜV Rheinland AG on June 15, 2024, valid through June 14, 2027. The certification covers Stratosphere\'s cloud hosting and managed database services operations at its Frankfurt, Germany and Dublin, Ireland data centers.

> \(b\) **SOC 2 Type II** --- Service Organization Controls Report. Report dated September 30, 2024, covering the audit period from October 1, 2023 through September 30, 2024, issued by Clearwater Audit Partners GmbH (Munich). The report covers the Trust Services Criteria of Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, and Confidentiality.

Stratosphere shall maintain its ISO/IEC 27001 certification in good standing and shall provide updated SOC 2 Type II reports to Pinnacle on an annual basis throughout the term of the MSA. Any material changes to the scope of Stratosphere\'s certifications or any failure to maintain or renew such certifications shall be promptly communicated to Pinnacle in writing.
**[Section 11 --- Termination]{.underline}**

**Termination for Material Breach:** Either party may terminate the MSA upon written notice to the other party if the other party commits a material breach of the MSA and fails to cure such breach within thirty (30) days after receipt of written notice specifying the nature of the breach in reasonable detail.

**Termination for Insolvency:** Either party may terminate the MSA immediately upon written notice if the other party becomes insolvent, makes an assignment for the benefit of creditors, files or has filed against it a petition in bankruptcy or similar proceeding, or has a receiver or trustee appointed for a substantial portion of its assets.

**Termination for Convenience by Client:** The Client may terminate the MSA for convenience upon ninety (90) days\' prior written notice to Stratosphere, subject to payment of all fees for services rendered through the effective date of termination and payment of fees for the remainder of the then-current quarterly invoicing period.

**Post-Termination Obligations:** Upon expiration or termination of the MSA for any reason, the parties\' post-termination obligations shall include transition assistance, data return, and data deletion, in each case as further specified in the DPA and the applicable Statements of Work.
**[Section 12 --- Miscellaneous]{.underline}**

**Entire Agreement:** The MSA, together with all exhibits thereto (including the DPA once executed as Exhibit D), all Statements of Work, and all written amendments and modifications, constitutes the entire agreement between the parties with respect to the subject matter hereof and supersedes all prior and contemporaneous negotiations, understandings, representations, and agreements, whether written or oral.

**Amendment:** The MSA may be amended, modified, or supplemented only by a written instrument duly executed by authorized representatives of both parties. No waiver of any provision of the MSA shall be effective unless made in writing and signed by the party granting such waiver.

**Notices:** All notices, demands, and other communications required or permitted under the MSA shall be in writing and shall be deemed duly given when delivered personally, sent by nationally recognized overnight courier, or sent by registered or certified mail (return receipt requested), addressed as follows:
> If to **Pinnacle:** Margaret Yuen-Park, General Counsel Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc. 4200 Harborview Boulevard, Suite 1100 Austin, TX 78746
> If to **Stratosphere:** Dr. Florian Neumann, Chief Legal Officer Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH Hohenzollernstraße 88 80796 Munich, Germany

**Assignment:** Neither party may assign or transfer its rights or obligations under the MSA without the prior written consent of the other party, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed; provided, however, that either party may assign the MSA without the other party\'s consent in connection with a merger, consolidation, reorganization, or sale of all or substantially all of the assigning party\'s assets, so long as the assignee agrees in writing to be bound by the terms of the MSA.

**Counterparts and Electronic Signatures:** The MSA may be executed in one or more counterparts, each of which shall be deemed an original and all of which together shall constitute one and the same instrument. The parties agree that electronic signatures shall have the same legal force and effect as original ink signatures.

Orionis provides anonymization and analytics services to Stratosphere in connection with the processing of EU personal data. Orionis operates exclusively from its Dublin location within the EEA.

77: **Note for legal review regarding Orionis:** The DPA Template describes Orionis\'s services as \"anonymization and analytics.\" However, the DPA does not define or distinguish between \"anonymization\" and \"pseudonymization.\" This omission creates significant regulatory ambiguity. Under the GDPR, truly anonymized data falls outside the scope of the Regulation entirely (Recital 26), meaning that once data has been effectively and irreversibly anonymized, no GDPR obligations attach to its further processing, storage, or transfer. By contrast, pseudonymized data remains personal data subject to the full scope of GDPR obligations (Article 4(5), Recital 26).
78: 
79: The standard for effective anonymization established in Article 29 Working Party Opinion 05/2014 on Anonymisation Techniques (WP216, now endorsed by the European Data Protection Board) requires that data be rendered irreversibly incapable of identifying a data subject, considering all means reasonably likely to be used. The WP29 Opinion establishes a three-criteria test assessing the risks of (i) singling out, (ii) linkability, and (iii) inference. Data that does not satisfy all three criteria cannot be considered truly anonymized.
80: 
81: If Orionis\'s processing produces pseudonymized rather than truly anonymized outputs, those outputs remain personal data subject to the GDPR and must be covered by the DPA\'s processing terms. This includes all obligations related to international transfer mechanisms (if the data were subsequently transferred outside the EEA), security measures, data retention limitations, data subject rights facilitation, and breach notification. The DPA should define the anonymization standard by reference to objective and verifiable criteria, specify validation and certification requirements for Orionis\'s outputs, and expressly address the regulatory consequences if true anonymization is not achieved in practice.

163: **Flow Description:**
164: 
165: The primary US data flow originates at **Pinnacle Health Solutions, Inc.** (Austin, TX), acting in its capacity as HIPAA Covered Entity and Controller. US patient PHI and US healthcare provider contact data are transmitted via encrypted connection using TLS 1.3 to a single destination within the United States:
166: 
167: **Destination:** The data is transmitted to the **Northern Virginia Data Center** located in Fairfax, Virginia, which is owned and operated by **Larkfield Data Systems, LLC**. Larkfield acts as a Subprocessor under the GDPR framework and as a Business Associate sub-contractor under HIPAA. Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH accesses and manages the data hosted at the Larkfield Northern Virginia facility pursuant to the terms of the MSA.

The adequacy of this BAA flow-down is addressed in the separate compliance gap memorandum and is not within the scope of this data flow document.

175: **[3.3 Diagram 3 --- Cross-Border Transfer: Frankfurt to Northern Virginia (Disaster Recovery)]{.underline}**
176: 
177: **Flow Description:**
178: 
179: This data flow involves the transfer of EU-originating data from within the EEA to a facility located in the United States. It constitutes an international transfer of personal data under GDPR Chapter V and requires a valid transfer mechanism.
180: 
181: **Source:** The data originates from the **Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH Frankfurt Data Center** (Frankfurt, Germany), where Stratosphere acts as Processor within the EEA. The datasets transferred consist of aggregated and pseudonymized datasets derived from EU personal data originally provided by Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V.
182: 
183: **Transmission:** The data is transmitted via encrypted connection to the destination facility. The DPA Template does not specify the encryption protocol for this particular transfer; counsel should confirm that TLS 1.3 or equivalent encryption is applied.
184: 
185: **Destination:** The data is received at the **Northern Virginia Data Center** (Fairfax, VA), operated by **Larkfield Data Systems, LLC**. Larkfield acts as Subprocessor. The data center is located outside the European Economic Area.
186: 
187: **Purpose:** Disaster recovery and business continuity. The transferred datasets are maintained at the Northern Virginia facility to ensure service continuity in the event of a catastrophic failure at the Frankfurt or Dublin data centers.
188: 
189: **Transfer Mechanism in DPA Template:** The DPA Template (Section 7) references the EU Standard Contractual Clauses adopted pursuant to Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 of June 4, 2021. However, the DPA Template attaches only **Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor)** of the 2021 SCCs.
190: 
191: **FLAG FOR LEGAL REVIEW --- Transfer Mechanism Gap :** This transfer is from **Stratosphere (Processor)** to **Larkfield (Subprocessor)**. The DPA Template attaches only SCC Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor), which governs transfers from a Controller to a Processor. However, this specific transfer is a Processor-to-Subprocessor transfer, which requires **SCC Module 3 (Processor-to-Subprocessor)** under Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914. The 2021 SCCs contain four modules designed for distinct transfer scenarios: Module 1 (Controller-to-Controller), Module 2 (Controller-to-Processor), Module 3 (Processor-to-Subprocessor), and Module 4 (Processor-to-Controller). Module 2 alone is legally insufficient for this transfer scenario. Module 3 must be separately executed between Stratosphere (as data exporter/Processor) and Larkfield (as data importer/Subprocessor), with Pinnacle Health Solutions EU B.V. as the ultimate Controller having enforceable rights under the SCCs as a third-party beneficiary. The failure to include Module 3 means there is currently no valid transfer mechanism in place for this data flow.
192: 
193: **FLAG FOR LEGAL REVIEW --- Larkfield DPF Status :** Larkfield Data Systems, LLC is **NOT** certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. The European Commission\'s adequacy decision for the DPF (adopted July 10, 2023) can only be relied upon where the data importer is a certified participant in the DPF program. Because Larkfield has not obtained DPF certification, the DPF adequacy decision cannot serve as an alternative transfer mechanism for this transfer. SCCs (with the correct Module 3 selection) remain the only viable mechanism for this transfer, unless Larkfield obtains DPF certification prior to the September 1, 2025 go-live date.
194: 
195: **FLAG FOR LEGAL REVIEW --- No Transfer Impact Assessment :** The DPA Template does not require, reference, or document any Transfer Impact Assessment (\"TIA\") for this transfer. Following the Court of Justice of the European Union\'s judgment in *Data Protection Commissioner v. Facebook Ireland Limited and Maximillian Schrenk* (Case C-311/18, \"Schrems II,\" July 16, 2020) and the EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 on measures that supplement transfer tools to ensure compliance with the EU level of protection of personal data (Version 2.0, adopted June 18, 2021), a TIA is required to assess whether the legal framework in the destination country (here, the United States) provides an essentially equivalent level of protection for personal data. The TIA must specifically assess US surveillance laws (including Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act and Executive Order 12333), the availability of redress mechanisms (including those established by Executive Order 14086 and the Data Protection Review Court), and any supplementary technical, organizational, or contractual measures needed to address identified risks. No TIA has been prepared, referenced, or required by the DPA Template for any international transfer.
196: 
197: **Additional Note Regarding Pseudonymized Data:** Although the datasets transferred to the Northern Virginia facility are described in the DPA Template as \"aggregated and pseudonymized,\" it is essential to recognize that pseudonymized data remains personal data under the GDPR (Article 4(5), Recital 26) and requires a valid transfer mechanism under Chapter V. Only data that has been truly and irreversibly anonymized in accordance with the standard articulated in WP29 Opinion 05/2014 (WP216) would fall outside the scope of the GDPR and thereby not require a transfer mechanism. The characterization of data as \"pseudonymized\" does not reduce or eliminate the requirement for SCCs or another valid transfer mechanism. See also the flag regarding Orionis and the anonymization/pseudonymization distinction in Section 1.3 above.
198: 
199: **[3.4 Diagram 4 --- Cross-Border Access: Singapore Remote Access to EU Data]{.underline}**
200: 
201: **Flow Description:**
202: 
203: This data flow involves remote access by Stratosphere personnel located outside the EEA to EU personal data stored within the EEA. Although no data is physically transferred to or stored in Singapore, remote access from a third country constitutes a \"transfer\" of personal data under the GDPR, as confirmed by EDPB guidance.
204: 
205: **Accessor:** **Stratosphere Cloud Services GmbH support engineers based in Singapore.** These individuals are employees or contractors of Stratosphere acting in their capacity as Processor personnel. Singapore is not an EU Member State and is not part of the European Economic Area.
206: 
207: **Access Method:** Remote access via encrypted VPN tunnel using TLS 1.3 to the Frankfurt and/or Dublin data centers. The Singapore-based engineers access EU personal data for the purposes of incident resolution and technical support. Data is viewed and, in some cases, modified remotely but is not copied to or stored at any Singapore facility.
208: 
209: **Data Location:** The EU personal data remains physically stored at the **Stratosphere Frankfurt Data Center** (Germany) and/or the **Stratosphere Dublin Data Center** (Ireland), both within the EEA.
210: 
211: **Purpose:** Incident resolution, technical troubleshooting, and technical support services.
212: 
213: **Nature of Access as International Transfer:** Although the data is not physically relocated to Singapore, remote access from a third country to personal data stored within the EEA constitutes an international transfer under the GDPR within the meaning of Chapter V. The EDPB has consistently treated such remote access scenarios as transfers requiring a valid legal mechanism. Singapore is not covered by an EU adequacy decision under Article 45 GDPR.
